Greeks Engine: adjoint-differentiated option Greeks on FPGAs

Complete technical dossier · Yash Agrawal, Birla Institute of Technology and Science, Pilani · Supervisor: Prof. Govind Prasad · Course registered under: Prof. Natasha Hazarika · 25 October 2026

A fixed-point FPGA engine that computes the Heston option price and all nine of its sensitivities (the Greeks) in one forward and one reverse (adjoint) pass of the COS Fourier pricer. It is produced by a generator that, from one description of the computation, emits a bit-accurate model, a first-order rounding-error bound for every output, a modulo-scheduled Verilog datapath and the host code. The engine has run on a ZedBoard (Zynq-7020) and, as a 64-bit configuration computing everything on chip, on a ZCU102 (Zynq UltraScale+), with every output bit-exact against the model on both.

1. Problem and motivation

A desk that holds options needs not only their prices but their Greeks: the derivatives of the price with respect to every input (spot, strike, maturity, rate and the model's parameters). They drive hedging, risk limits and model calibration, and must be recomputed whenever the market moves.

Under the Heston stochastic-volatility model there is no closed-form price; it is computed numerically, here by the COS Fourier-cosine method. The standard way to get Greeks is bump-and-reprice: change one input slightly and price again. Nine Greeks by central differences cost 19 pricings, and the result depends on a bump size with no safe choice (too small and rounding dominates, too large and truncation does).

Adjoint (reverse-mode) differentiation computes every derivative of one output in a single backward sweep, at a small constant multiple of one pricing, independent of the number of inputs. In software it is the industry standard for Greeks, but it records a tape of the computation and replays it, which costs 3–7 pricings in practice and is memory-bound. Published FPGA Greeks engines do not use adjoints at all: they re-run the pricer once per sensitivity (Section 7).

The idea: the COS pricer performs exactly the same operations for every input, so its adjoint can be written once, compiled into a fixed hardware schedule with no tape, and executed on arithmetic units that the forward pass leaves idle.

2. System model

2.1 The Heston model

The asset price S and its instantaneous variance v evolve under the risk-neutral measure as

dSt = r St dt + √vt St dW1,    dvt = κ(θ − vt) dt + ξ √vt dW2,    dW1 dW2 = ρ dt

with nine inputs: spot S0, strike K, maturity T, rate r, initial variance v0, mean-reversion speed κ, long-run variance θ, volatility of variance ξ and correlation ρ. The verified input domain is S0 = 100, K ∈ [60, 150], T ∈ [0.1, 3], r ∈ [0, 0.1], v0, θ ∈ [0.005, 0.25], κ ∈ [0.2, 6], ξ ∈ [0.1, 1], ρ ∈ [−0.95, 0.6]; outside it the hardware raises range_err instead of returning a wrong value.

The log-price characteristic function, in the numerically stable form used throughout, with x = ln(S0/K):

d = √[ (κ − iρξu)2 + ξ2(u2 + iu) ],    g = (κ − iρξu − d) / (κ − iρξu + d)
φ(u) = exp{ iu(x + rT) + (κθ/ξ2)[ (κ − iρξu − d)T − 2 ln((1 − ge−dT)/(1 − g)) ] + (v0/ξ2)(κ − iρξu − d)(1 − e−dT)/(1 − ge−dT) }

2.2 COS pricing

The COS method (Fang & Oosterlee) expands the density on a truncation range [a, b] in a cosine series whose coefficients come from the characteristic function:

V ≈ K e−rT Σ′k=0N−1 Re[ φ(uk) e−iuka ] Vk,    uk = kπ/(b − a),    [a, b] = c1 ± 10√c2,    N = 128

where Σ′ halves the first term, c1, c2 are the first two cumulants and Vk are the cosine coefficients of the put payoff (closed form in χk, ψk). Calls are priced as puts plus put-call parity, C = P + S0 − Ke−rT, because a call's coefficients carry eb, which grows and then cancels and loses precision in fixed point.

2.3 The Greeks

The engine returns the price and nine sensitivities: delta ∂V/∂S0, ∂V/∂K, theta ∂V/∂T, rho ∂V/∂r, vega ∂V/∂v0, and ∂V/∂κ, ∂V/∂θ, ∂V/∂ξ, ∂V/∂ρ. As is standard for COS, the derivatives are of the COS approximation with the truncation range [a, b] held fixed. Each term contributes Re[φ(uk)·...]; the parameters enter only through the exponent of φ, so the adjoint sweep is seeded by the adjoint of that exponent and runs back through d, g, the logarithm and the exponentials to the eight inputs T, r, v0, κ, θ, ξ, ρ and x; delta and ∂V/∂K follow from ∂V/∂x in the finish step.

2.4 Adjoint (reverse-mode) differentiation

Write the computation as a sequence of elementary operations vj = fj(vi, ...). The adjoint of each intermediate, v̄i = ∂y/∂vi, is accumulated backwards:

ȳ = 1,    v̄i = Σj: i→j v̄j ∂fj/∂vi,    ∇y = (x̄1, ..., x̄n)

so one backward sweep gives the derivative with respect to every input, at a cost that is a small constant multiple of the forward pass whatever the number of inputs. Software tools record the operations on a tape and replay it. Here the graph is the same for every input, so the reverse sweep is written once as operations of the same graph (hardware/gen/heston.py), shares reciprocals and other values with the forward pass, and is scheduled statically: no tape and no replay logic. The adjoint is derived by hand at the complex-arithmetic level and verified against forward mode and finite differences; making the generator derive it automatically is planned work.

2.5 Fixed-point arithmetic and the first-order error bound

Every value is an integer times 2−FL: the Zynq-7020 engine uses 56-bit words with 28 fraction bits, the 64-bit engine 64-bit words with 32. Normalised quantities (reciprocals, logarithms, CORDIC) use their own mantissa formats; data-dependent shifts are built only as wide as the ranges measured over the verified domain (with margin), which saves about a third of the logic, and any input that would exceed them sets range_err. Division, square root, exponential and logarithm are built from shared multipliers (Newton–Raphson reciprocals, Tang-style exponentials) and CORDIC units.

Each operation i rounds its result by at most εi (half a unit in its last place). To first order the error of an output y is bounded by

| ŷ − y | ≤ Σi | ∂y/∂vi | εi    (products of rounding errors, O(2−2FL), dropped)

The sensitivities ∂y/∂vi come from a second reverse sweep over the rounding model of the whole datapath, including the hardware's own adjoint, so every Greek gets its own bound in about 0.1 s per parameter set. The bound covers fixed-point rounding against the same algorithm computed exactly; the COS method's own truncation error is a separate term (Section 5.4).

3. Architecture

3.1 Design flow

One description of the computation (an operation graph with a fixed-point format on every node) produces the emulator, the bound, the schedule, the Verilog and the host C; verify_all.sh checks each artifact against the others.

3.2 Inside the engine

The per-evaluation setup computes the truncation range, grid spacing and every quantity that does not depend on the term index. The term loop runs the 128 COS terms through one pipelined datapath: each term computes its payoff coefficient and characteristic function (forward), then the adjoint sweep, and adds its contribution to nine sums. A modulo scheduler starts a new term every II cycles on a fixed set of shared units; term k uses unit u at phase (t − S) mod II, values living longer than II get register chains, and about 16 terms are in flight at once. On the Zynq-7020 configuration the CORDIC units set II = 32, which leaves multiplier slots idle in the forward pass; the adjoint's multiplies fill them, so the Greeks cost only 165 extra cycles. The finish discounts the sums, applies the chain rule for delta and ∂V/∂K, and adds put-call parity for calls.

DesignWordMultipliersCORDICSetup/finishCyclesTarget

One parameter (the number of shared multipliers) moves the design between a small engine for a low-cost FPGA and a fast one for a large FPGA (Section 5.1).

3.4 Board systems

All three systems use generated AXI4-Lite register files around the engine (the AXI4-Stream wrappers, up to 1,456 bits wide, are too wide for any Zynq processor port). In A and C the PC drives the bus over JTAG through Vivado, so the only thing under test is the engine. In B the ARM computes the setup and finish steps as C generated from the same graph, bit-exact with the model on 300 inputs including the portable 64×64→128-bit multiply the 32-bit ARM needs, and times every stage with the Cortex-A9 global timer.

3.5 Verification

verify_all.sh runs 25 automated checks: arithmetic primitives within 2.5–4 ULP; the first-generation engines; every generated datapath bit-exact against the emulator at the register level and its cycle count equal to the schedule; out-of-domain inputs raising range_err; every AXI wrapper bit-exact; host steps + FPGA loop equal to the on-chip design; the committed RTL equal to the generator's output; the host C bit-exact with two arithmetic paths; the ARM program on a register model (100 cases); and the emulator's accuracy and bound. Board scripts are tested against a model of Vivado's hardware manager with injected faults.

4. Novelty claims

Literature checks on 29 September and 6 October 2026 (full texts searched where available; docs/novelty_assessment.md) found no prior work for claims 1 and 2.

  1. The first FPGA implementation of adjoint (reverse-mode) differentiation for option Greeks. Every published FPGA Greeks engine re-runs the pricer once per sensitivity; the 2024 survey of 99 FPGA option-pricing studies and the 2024 review of fifteen years of adjoint differentiation in finance contain no FPGA adjoint implementation. Wording keep “adjoint” and “for option Greeks”: forward-mode AD has run in an FPGA soft processor (Schoder & Bücker), so “first AD on an FPGA” would be false.
  2. The first FPGA implementation of the COS method. COS had run on CPUs and GPUs; the only FPGA Fourier pricer (AMD's hcfEngine) uses trapezoidal integration and returns the price alone.
  3. A tape-free adjoint datapath. The reverse sweep is compiled into a statically scheduled fixed-point datapath that shares its units with the forward pass, possible because the COS pricer's graph does not depend on its inputs.
  4. All nine Greeks for 1.04 pricings, with the fewest multipliers. Forward-mode datapaths built by the same generator need more multiplies for the same Greeks: 313 per term hand-factored like analytic Greeks and 802 as an AD tool would build them, against the adjoint's 250; reaching the same pace takes 10 and 26 multipliers against 8. Wording the 1.04× itself is not unique (with 16 multipliers the factored forward method also reaches it); the claim is fewer DSP blocks for the same speed.
  5. A first-order rounding-error bound for every Greek of a fixed-point adjoint datapath, never exceeded: worst 0.103 of the bound over 21 cases, 0.378 over 10,500 inputs, 0.356 over 10,500 held-out inputs, 0.24 against a 50-digit evaluation, 0.199 on the ZedBoard and 0.255 on the ZCU102. Wording “first-order” and “rounding only”; the method builds on Linnainmaa (1976).
  6. Bit-exact Greeks on silicon, on two FPGA families: 450 of 450 outputs of 50 random cases on a ZedBoard, run twice on successive designs; 1,010 of 1,010 for the 64-bit engine on a ZCU102 (1 vector, 50 random cases, 50 real NIFTY days).
  7. A generator for fixed-point adjoint datapaths that emits the emulator, bound, schedule, Verilog, wrappers and host C from one description (tool contribution; Pham et al. 2016 generated Monte Carlo pricers without Greeks).
Not claimed: a latency win on the Zynq-7020 (the CPU is 3.2× faster there), or more than a narrow one on the ZCU102 (1.3×); throughput against a multi-core CPU; a statistical hedging result; a measured (rather than simulated) energy figure, until the board and CPU measurements are done.

Worst relative error against the same algorithm in double precision over 21 parameter sets spanning moneyness, maturity, vol-of-vol, correlation, calls and puts.

Over the whole domain (validation/run_domain_sweep.py): 6,000 uniform inputs, 500 in each of seven hard regimes (Feller-violating, extreme correlation, deep strikes, short and long maturities, high vol-of-vol, very low variance) and 1,000 out-of-domain inputs. The bound held in every unflagged result (worst 0.378), with no overflow. A held-out sweep of the same size with a fresh seed (the ranges were refitted after the first) gave no in-domain flag and a worst of 0.356.

Significant figures against double precision (9,500 held-out in-domain inputs): price, delta, strike, theta, rho and vega ≥ 5.3 in 99% of inputs (median 7.6–8.1, worst 3.3–4.4); ∂V/∂θ, ∂V/∂ρ 4.9; ∂V/∂κ and ∂V/∂ξ only 3.5 and 3.0 (worst 2.2 and 1.4 where they are small).

The bound is first order. A 50-digit evaluation of the same graph on 100 held-out inputs put the hardware's error at most 0.24 of the bound, identical to three decimals to the figure against double precision; the bound also held at 44 bits, where second-order terms are relatively 4,096 times larger.

5.11 Many strikes at once (design study)

All strikes of one expiry share the COS grid, so one characteristic function and one adjoint sweep per term serve every strike; each extra strike costs 16 multiplies and one rotation per term (about 7% of one option). Scheduled and emulated, not built:

StrikesZ7-style cyclesper strike64-bit cyclesper strike
14,6624,6621,5771,577

168,7675482,854178
3212,8604024,892153

The same sharing helps a CPU as much (2.3 µs per strike at 32 strikes on one idle core), and pricing many strikes from one characteristic function is standard COS practice, so this is a design result, not a novelty claim.

5.12 Illustration: hedging on real NIFTY data

Twelve short at-the-money NIFTY call trades (Sep 2025 – Sep 2026, NSE end-of-day data, real quotes only), hedged daily with futures after every Indian charge and 30% tax, with the Heston model calibrated each day to about 170 real option prices. Spread of profit and loss per trade: unhedged ₹5.55 L, Black–Scholes delta ₹2.05 L, Heston delta ₹2.50 L, and the minimum-variance hedge (delta plus ρξ/S·vega, two Greeks from the same pass) ₹1.26 L.

An illustration, not evidence for the hardware: the hedge decisions come from the hedging formula, are insensitive to word length (48-bit deltas trade the same lots), and a double-precision CPU would trade the same lots. Twelve trades give about 88% bootstrap confidence. The 50 trading days' calibrated parameters are ready as board vectors for both boards.

7. Comparison with published work

Published FPGA finance work is mostly Monte Carlo pricing over large batches, reported as batch runtime or energy against multi-core servers; this work evaluates one option at a time by a Fourier method. Those numbers measure different things and are not directly comparable; the table positions the works by what they compute and how, with each paper's own headline figure where it was read from the source.

Schoder & Bücker, 2024/25Alveo U50 (RISC-V soft core)General programsForward-mode AD in the processor–AD in FPGA hardware, no finance
Boudaoud et al. (DaCe AD), 2025CPU, GPU (FPGA back end not evaluated)GeneralReverse-mode AD framework–No finance
O Mahony et al., survey 2024 (99 studies); Capriotti & Giles, review 2024––No FPGA adjoint implementation in either–Establish the gap
Where this work stands: it is the only entry that computes Greeks on an FPGA by an adjoint, the only FPGA COS implementation, and the only one with a guaranteed per-Greek rounding bound and a bit-exact silicon result. It does not compete on batch throughput with large Alveo Monte Carlo designs; its comparable quantities are the cost of the Greeks relative to a price, their accuracy, and latency and energy per evaluation.

8. Limitations

  • Board runs pending for the ZedBoard processor system (bus-transfer timing) and its NIFTY run. The ZCU102 latency is the cycle count at the clock: the board run checks every output but JTAG cannot time the engine.
  • CPU power estimated from the part's rated 12–28 W (CPU timings are measured, on an idle machine).
  • Power is simulated, engine only: no clock generator, bus or board; a supply measurement is pending. 57% of nets were matched by name, the rest propagated.
  • Latency: on the Zynq-7020 one laptop core with hand-derived Greeks is 3.2× faster (timing does not close at 100 MHz there, Fmax ~79 MHz); on the ZCU102 the engine leads by only 1.3×, and four cores give 2.5× its throughput.
  • The bound is first order and covers rounding only; the COS method's own error is separate and reaches 7.8×10−3 on vega in the worst board case.
  • ∂V/∂κ and ∂V/∂ξ carry only about 3 significant figures at the 99th percentile.
  • The adjoint is hand-derived (verified, not generated by an AD tool); say “adjoint differentiation”.
  • Bounded input domain; outside it the hardware raises range_err.
  • Hedging is an illustration with 12 trades; charge rates still to be checked with a broker.

10. Reproducing the results

cd "Greek Engine"
./verify_all.sh                                    # 25 checks: RTL, wrappers, host C, bound
.venv/bin/python validation/run_mode_baselines.py  # adjoint vs forward mode
.venv/bin/python validation/run_domain_sweep.py [--heldout]   # 10,500-input sweeps
.venv/bin/python validation/sigfig_report.py       # significant figures
.venv/bin/python validation/run_mp_check.py 100    # 50-digit check of the bound
.venv/bin/python validation/run_method_error.py    # COS method error
.venv/bin/python validation/cpu_baseline/run_baseline.py      # CPU comparison
hardware/vivado/zedboard/run_board.bat build | test | sweep | nifty | ps
hardware/vivado/zcu104/run_board.bat   build | test | sweep | nifty
hardware/vivado/zcu102/run_board.sh    dry | build | test | sweep | nifty   (Linux; make_bundle.py packs it)
.venv/bin/python validation/board_report.py <log> --design zu [--cases-csv ...]   # error vs bound on silicon
hardware/sw/zedboard: vitis -s build_vitis.py ; xsdb run_app.tcl
hardware/vivado/power: run_engine_power.tcl <top> <part> <clk_ns>

Key files: hardware/gen/ (graph, emulator, bound, scheduler, generators), hardware/verilog/gen/ (generated RTL), validation/results/ (every number above), docs/report/latex/ (the project report), docs/architecture.md and docs/novelty_assessment.md (detailed notes).
